title: A Stroll Through Georgetown - In Person
desc: Established 50 years before Washington, D.C., Georgetown got its start as a gritty port city on the banks of the Potomac River. Despite its modest beginnings, Georgetown eventually came to have some of the most expensive and desirable property in the District. Join Carolyn Muraskin, founder of DC Design Tours, for a walk through one of D.C.’s most exclusive neighborhoods, home to palatial mansions, elegant cemeteries, stately churches, and a world-class university.

title: Death and Beyond: Comparative Reflections in World Religious Traditions
desc: Issues of death, dying, love, and the meaning life—and the afterlife—hold key places in the belief systems of the major religious traditions of the world. Graham M. Schweig , a professor of philosophy and religion at Christopher Newport University, leads a seminar that surveys differing visions of these timeless themes from a variety of Eastern and Western cultural-religious perspectives.

title: Inside the Folger Shakespeare Library - In Person
desc: Go behind the scenes at the Folger Shakespeare Library for a day of rare books, scintillating conversation, and live theater centered on one of Shakespeare’s most provocative plays, Measure for Measure. Staff members provide a guided introduction to the Folger and its renowned collections—which include 82 First Folios—along with a tour of the recently renovated building. Enjoy a special session that offers insights into the play before the matinee and a private discussion with Folger production staff afterward.

title: Broad Stripes and Bright Stars
desc: Meet Mary Pickersgill, seamstress of the enormous garrison flag that inspired the lyrics to America’s national anthem and later became known as the Star-Spangled Banner. What was it like to live in a nation defending its sovereignty? Learn about the War of 1812, considered America’s Second War of Independence, and about ways that widows like Mary expressed patriotism and resourcefulness through acquired skills and family connections.

desc: A stunning example of rural Gothic architecture and Georgia’s centuries-old Episcopal infrastructure, Zion Church in Talbotton has stood at the heart of the state’s historical and cultural preservation efforts for many years. Its annual Talbotton Blues Festival is one of the many fundraising and culture-sustaining events produced by Zion Church Restoration, Inc. and the Georgia Trust for Historic Preservation, and features local artisans, cooks, and blues musicians.

Together, these programs remind us that the journey toward a more perfect union begins with listening, sharing, and creating solutions together. Featured artists : Maestro Francesco Mamola and Alfonzo Brandi (guitarist). Presented in partnership with the N.O.I. Foundation (Nuovi Orizzonti Italiani).

title: SHOUT
desc: Join our ensemble of performers as they sing, dance, and teach through storytelling. Learn about the ring shout—a powerful practice blending song and rhythmic movement created by enslaved communities in the 1700s and 1800s. They combined various religious practices of Europe and Africa, creating a cultural tradition that became iconically American. Connect their syncopated musical rhythms from the past to the present and learn how music can be a form of joyful resistance in times of oppression.

title: Tour | Art & Architecture
desc: Explore the architecture of the National Mall’s first art museum on this tour of the National Museum of Asian Art's Freer Gallery. Look closely at the West Building’s plaza, lobby, and inner courtyard while discovering the Italian architectural influences and design details of this US National Historic Landmark designed by the famed turn-of-the-century architect Charles Platt. Please meet at the West Building plaza for the tour. During rainy weather, meet at the West Building information desk . Image credit: National Museum of Asian Art, Smithsonian Institution. Photo by Jennifer Berry.

title: Tour | From the Louvre
desc: In From the Louvre: Masterpieces of Islamic Art , you can admire remarkable artworks created between the seventh and nineteenth centuries from a vast geographic area extending from Spain to India. This tour guides you through the exceptional selection of masterpieces, including a striking Syrian-Egyptian basin inlaid with silver figures, an enigmatic Andalusian bronze lion, and a monumental portrait of a Persian king covered with jewels. Meanwhile, learn about the extraordinary journeys these works took and how they were invested with power and new meaning along the way. Image: Signed by Muham

title: Ogen: Anchoring Together Cultivating a Practice of Resilience
desc: “Ogen” is Hebrew for “anchor.” This six-week workshop is an invitation to cultivate a practice of resilience with insight and connection, anchoring our week with 30 minutes of Jewish wisdoms of self-awareness and emotional precision. Join us on Mondays at 12pm ET from Jan 26-Mar 2. Come when you can. Attend all sessions, or join us for the ones you can. Taught by beloved SVIVAH educator, Dr. Naama Sadan, Ogen offers a much-needed space to explore resilience through the spiritual teachings of Yemima Avital, renowned feminist psycho/spiritual scholar and educator.

title: Churchill and the Crown
desc: Winston Churchill’s political career began when Queen Victoria was on the throne and ended during the reign of Elizabeth II. His experience over half a century at the forefront of British politics made him an indispensable adviser upon the accession of the young queen—whom he first met as a 2-year-old princess. Katherine Carter , curator of Churchill’s country home at Chartwell, shares the history of this remarkable friendship.

title: Before Baker Street: Joseph Bell and the Making of Sherlock Holmes
desc: Sherlock Holmes is known the world over, yet the man Arthur Conan Doyle credited as Sherlock’s prototype is unsung. The deductive powers of 19th-century doctor Joseph Bell—who read patients’ ailments, occupation, and personal habits at a single glance—had a profound influence on medical student Conan Doyle. Author Lindsey Fitzharris recounts how Bell’s work took him from ward to witness box as a medical detective.

title: Pinacoteca Nazionale di Bologna
desc: In the historic university city of Bologna, the Pinacoteca Nazionale di Bologna houses one of Italy’s most important collections of Renaissance painting. Among its treasures are masterpieces by Giotto, Raphael, and Parmigianino, as well as of the Bolognese school. Italian Renaissance art expert Rocky Ruggiero discusses the significance of this extraordinary collection and the enduring legacy of Bologna’s artistic tradition. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: The Geology of Yellowstone: Past, Present and Future
desc: The Yellowstone Caldera, formed 630,000 years ago, anchors America’s first national park, yet Yellowstone’s volcanic story stretches back 17 million years and continues today, notes volcanologist Kirt Kempter . He guides participants through the park’s geology, from unique rocks to hydrothermal features, using Google Earth views, diagrams, maps, and field photos to reveal how ongoing volcanic and geothermal forces shape Yellowstone’s dramatic landscape.

How to Read a Film
desc: Humanities scholar Clay Jenkinson reminds viewers that films are built from thousands of creative choices, and understanding them means examining elements like pace, music, lighting, direction, acting styles, and editing. Learning to isolate these components deepens appreciation without diminishing enjoyment. Jenkinson illustrates his approach through two films from Christopher Nolan, Oppenheimer and The Odyssey, and Philip Kaufman's The Right Stuff .

title: The Language of 1776
desc: In 1776, Americans were not only fighting for political independence but also creating the conditions for new, distinctly American ways of speaking. Linguist Anne Curzan explores the state of the English language in the richly multilingual context of 18th-century America. Curzan traces the birth of Americanisms such as maize , backwoods , and bluff . She also illustrates how patterns of immigration shaped the American accents and dialects heard across regions and social groups today.

title: The Great Harry Houdini: Life, Death, and the Afterlife
desc: The death-defying escapes and daredevil stunts of Harry Houdini made him a sensation. But he created a new role for himself as an anti-spiritualist crusader in his later years, believing that so-called mediums who professed to make contact with the spirits of the departed were hucksters. Author Daniel Stashower explores Houdini’s life and legacy, while actors Scott Sedar and Bari Biern give voice to his career both onstage and in the séance room.

title: The Promised Land: Text, Tradition, and Interpretation
desc: INSIGHTS & IDEAS: TUESDAY NIGHT LEARNING WITH GIDEON AMIR August 4, 11, 18, 25 | 7-8:30 PM ET Location: Zoom Classroom God promised Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob that their descendants would inherit the land of Canaan. After the Exodus from Egypt and forty years of wandering in the desert, the Israelites, under Joshua’s leadership, conquered the Promised Land and settled there. However, the biblical text raises difficult geographical and ethical questions. Join us to explore these questions and examine how they have been understood and addressed across generations.

title: From Alliance to Friendship: Blacks, Jews and Pluralistic Peoplehood

title: Heresy: How the Search for the True Faith Shaped Christianity
desc: Throughout Christian history, followers of Christ have sought to define his message and the correct faith in God and the Trinity. From 42nd Street and Swing Time to Meet Me in St. Louis, West Side Story, and Chicago , the four-part series celebrates the songs, stars, and stories that made movie musicals an enduring part of American culture.

desc: In the years leading up to the Revolution, cartoons, newspapers, broadsides, and pamphlets created by patriots like Benjamin Franklin, Paul Revere, and Thomas Paine helped unsettle American loyalty to King George III and fueled the colonial Americans’ desire for independence. Stop by our reproduction eighteenth-century printing press to understand the historical connections between technology, communication, and democracy.

title: Autumn Scenes
desc: Hone your thematic skills and train your lens on classic fall scenes. Embrace the season by stepping out to snap picturesque landscapes, flame-colored foliage, and other autumnal sights from pumpkin patches and farm equipment to black cats and scarecrows.

title: Henri Matisse: An Enduring Fascination
desc: Henri Matisse is considered one of the most innovative and influential artists of the 20th century. Matisse’s oeuvre includes a wide range of materials and styles, but he is best-known for sensual, motion-infused canvases that pulsate with the intense light and vivid color of southern France. Art historian Nancy G. Heller examines these canvases and provides examples of how the artist’s work continues to fascinate. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: The American Colonies in the Age of Sail
desc: In the early 18th century, American colonists along the seaboard built and sailed small vessels in coastal trade. Growing Caribbean plantations needed provisions, prompting widespread smuggling that violated British, French, and Spanish mercantilist laws. Skilled American mariners, adept in shallow-water navigation, became ideal illicit traders. Historian Carl Herzog of the USS Constitution Museum argues that decades of defying imperial policies fostered professional networks, business savvy, and covert practices that ultimately helped sail colonists toward revolution.

title: Hidden Terrors in America: The 1830s Cholera Pandemic
desc: From 1832 to 1836, cholera swept through U.S. cities, towns, farms, prisons, and plantations, killing victims within hours and baffling Americans who lacked bacteriology. Though it struck all classes and regions, elites insisted it targeted only the supposedly immoral, blaming deaths among enslaved African Americans, Indigenous peoples, and Irish immigrants. As fatalities mounted, the universal threat became undeniable. Historian Paul Kelton reveals how this deadly germ collided with the social injustices of the era.

title: Orchids: Rooted in History
desc: Orchids aren’t just beautiful—they’re ancient survivors, with a lineage stretching back more than 120 million years. Over time, they’ve adapted to nearly every environment, evolving extraordinary forms and captivating people across cultures. Barb Schmidt , the vice president of the American Orchid Society, leads a journey through deep time, from orchids that grew alongside dinosaurs to the dazzling varieties of today. Schmidt explores their evolution, stories of daring orchid hunters, and the cultural meanings that have made these blooms so fascinating.

title: The Statue of Liberty: A Transatlantic Story
desc: When French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi first traveled to the United States to propose the construction of a giant tribute to liberty, Americans either rejected the idea or were baffled by it. Nevertheless, completed in 1886, the Statue of Liberty stands today as one of the best-known symbols of the United States. It was ultimately a gift from the French people to the American people, as private citizens, not the two governments, financed it from torch to toe. Historian Edward Berenson illuminates the origins of Lady Liberty, the complex construction process, and her shifting meaning.

title: Franklin D. Roosevelt and the Rise of Fascism
desc: Historian and author William I. Hitchcock argues that Americans were not simply indifferent to the rise of fascism before World War II. From Mussolini’s rise in 1922 to Pearl Harbor in 1941, the nation engaged in intense debates over the threat—and appeal—of authoritarianism. Initially focused on the New Deal and avoiding foreign conflicts, Franklin D. Roosevelt gradually recognized fascism’s dangers. Influenced by journalists, advisers, and activists, he helped build a coalition committed to defending democracy, human rights, and freedom worldwide.

title: Magna Graecia: Early Greek Culture in Italy
desc: In Plato’s time the South of Italy was known as “Greater Greece,” the beautiful land settled in the centuries after 800 B.C.E. by colonists from the Greek mainland. They also nurtured on Italian soil the political, philosophical, and artistic foundations that would influence and support the world of the Ancient Romans and, much later, that of the Italian Renaissance.

desc: In classical antiquity, Gibraltar inspired the original idea that the Earth was divided into distinct continents. Sailors, poets, and geographers saw Gibraltar as a natural marker separating the Mediterranean from the Atlantic and Europe from Africa. This idea had lasting global ramifications, and the geography of the Strait of Gibraltar helped create the pattern of European imperialism and the trajectory of the slave trade. title: Musical Innovation in the Age of AI
desc: Throughout history, new technologies have changed the ways people create, experiment, and bring ideas to life. Today, AI is becoming another tool in the creative process, giving songwriters new ways to improvise, explore possibilities, and develop variations on their ideas. What happens to the creative process when people collaborate with AI? How might new technologies change what it means to compose, invent, and create? In this free public program, a human-centered composer and an expert in computational creativity join a music journalist and critic to explore how AI is reshaping songwriting

title: By Illegitimate Means: How Birth Decides Dynasties
desc: Legitimacy in medieval and early modern England was never private. Birthright could reorder kingdoms and spark wars. Historian Cheryl White traces how disputed heirs shaped dynasties—from William the Conqueror, mocked as “the Bastard” yet able to seize a throne, to the crises after Edward III and the tenuous claim of Henry VII. White reveals how the fate of a kingdom could turn on one enduring question: Who was born to rule?

title: Gaudí's Vision: Heritage, Innovation, and the Future of Design
desc: As the world commemorates the 100th anniversary of Antoni Gaudí's death, explore the lasting influence of this visionary architect. Most of Gaudi’s Modernist designs are in or near Barcelona, Spain, and seven of them have been named UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Amilcar Vargas , head of heritage at Casa Batlló—a Gaudi masterpiece and UNESCO World Heritage Site—examines how the architect’s work inspires conversations about creativity, sustainability, craftsmanship, and the relationship between nature and the built environment. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: Virunga National Park
desc: The mist-enshrouded peaks of the Virunga Mountains, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, are part of one of Africa’s earliest protected natural areas. Known for an active chain of volcanoes, Virunga National Park is home to the endangered mountain gorilla and more than 300 other faunal and floral species. Historian Justin M. Jacobs shows how together with the adjacent lands of Volcanoes National Park, made famous by the fieldwork of zoologist Dian Fossey, Virunga provides a tense yet majestic backdrop for the competing demands of economic development and ecological preservation.

title: San Francisco: Then and Now
desc: Regional historian and master storyteller John Martini brings the past vividly into the present through the fascinating art of rephotography—the process of locating the exact vantage points of historic photographs and capturing those same scenes today. Using dozens of compelling “then-and-now” comparisons, Martini reveals how some of the Bay Area’s most famous landmarks, including Alcatraz Island, Fort Point, and Sutro Baths, have evolved across more than a century of dramatic change.

title: The American Table: 10 Cookbooks That Shaped a Nation
desc: Among the thousands of cookbooks published since the nation’s earliest days, a select few have transformed the way Americans cook, eat, and think about food. Cultural historian Leslie Goddard journeys through the pages of some of America’s most influential cookbooks, including ones by Fannie Farmer, Irma Rombauer, and Julia Child, and uncovers what they reveal about the evolution of American food culture.

title: J.M.W. Turner and John Constable: Rivals in the Romantic Era
desc: J.M.W. Turner and John Constable, two of Britain’s greatest painters, were contemporaries. title: Take a Seat!: Chairs of the 20th Century
desc: Many of the chairs still in use today were designed in the 20th century—and have stood the test of time for their comfort, function, and striking visual presence. Art historian Jennie Hirsh explores the history of iconic modern chairs from around the world, tracing how designers including Elaine Gray, Mies van der Rohe, Eero Saarinen, and Charles and Ray Eames reimagined seating for a rapidly changing century. ( World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: Meditation Mondays
desc: Join us for an in-person meditation on our 4th floor, Panoramic Overlook. This session provides an opportunity for participants of any experience level to explore the museum’s themes through mindfulness meditation practice. Together we will experience freedom in the present moment through insight into oneself. This session will be instructor led. No experience or special clothing is necessary. Seating will be provided. For inquiries, please contact NMAAHCEngage@si.edu

title: Double Victory: The African American Military Experience Highlights Tour

Visitors have an opportunity to engage in a conversation with a museum docent and learn about the contributions of African Americans to the military history of the United States. Tours take place at 1:15 pm and 2:30 pm.

title: The Art of Historic Preservation
desc: Historic preservation is often thought of as the stewardship of grand landmarks associated with great figures like Thomas Jefferson, as well as places of worship, courthouses, and monuments. But the modest houses, working landscapes, and overlooked spaces that hold our personal and collective memories also matter. Public historian Ken Turino traces the history of the preservation movement in America, including how the field has evolved to have a more inclusive vision of what deserves protection.

desc: Popular speaker and concert pianist Rachel Franklin explores the creative minds and keyboard talents of a quartet of piano pioneers celebrated for their prowess as both composers and performers. Franklin concludes each lecture by performing a work by the spotlighted composer.

title: A Fall Walk on Theodore Roosevelt Island - In Person
desc: Enjoy a fall morning walk on a natural oasis in the Potomac River with Melanie Choukas-Bradley , the author of Finding Solace at Theodore Roosevelt Island . The nearly 2-mile path follows Theodore Roosevelt Island’s shore and moves deep into the swamp and tidal inlet along the boardwalk where willows, bald cypresses, and cattails frame views of Washington, D.C. Choukas-Bradley gives an overview of the landscape’s mix of trees, wildflowers, birds, and other wildlife and highlights the island’s history and the legacy of the conservationist president it memorializes.

title: Big Objects, Big Stories: The Paradox of the Liberty
desc: Join us for a docent-led tour to get a fresh look into the Museum's featured object. At each of these 15-minute talks visitors will hear incredibly big stories about a big object. About this Program: The paradox of the American Revolution is the fight for liberty in an era of widespread slavery. Talk with a museum docent and explore the tension between slavery and freedom—who belongs and who is excluded. Consider how this paradox resonates through the nation’s history and spurs the American people to wrestle constantly with building “a more perfect Union.”

title: Shtürmer, Rasputin, and the Russian Revolution From Within
desc: In 1917, the Bolsheviks seized power after more than a year of unrest and Russia’s disastrous involvement in World War I. In 1916, Prime Minister Boris Shtürmer had raised the prospect of a separate peace with Germany to support his aspirations to power, and with Rasputin’s help, he contrived to stir up a crisis he could control. Historian and documentarian Indy Neidell examines the facts and myths behind these claims. Before any plan could succeed, however, Rasputin was dead, Shtürmer was imprisoned, and Russia plunged into revolution.

title: The Rise and Fall of Excommunication in Medieval England
desc: Excommunication was originally intended as a severe, rarely imposed punishment that excluded offenders from the sacraments, society, and certain legal rights. Over time, however, it became a routine tool used for political, legal, and personal ends. Historian Charlotte Whatley argues that English bishops increasingly relied on excommunication to resist royal authority, provoking conflict with King Edward III. The Crown ultimately weakened its coercive power, reinforcing the supremacy of English common law.

title: A History of the Movie Musical
desc: As soon as movies learned to talk, they also learned to sing and dance—and the movie musical quickly became one of America’s most popular film genres. Media historian Brian Rose guides you through the rich history of the movie musical, illustrated with extended clips from dozens of classic films. From 42nd Street and Swing Time to Meet Me in St. Louis, West Side Story, and Chicago , the four-part series celebrates the songs, stars, and stories that made movie musicals an enduring part of American culture.

title: Step into the World of M.C. Escher
desc: Maurits Cornelis Escher (1898–1972), popularly referred to as M.C. Escher, is known for what he called his “mental images,” which connect to mathematics and various branches of science. During his 50-year career, Escher’s works evolved from realistic observations of the world to inventions of his imagination that explored multidimensional alternate realities. Dena M. Woodall , a curator at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, explores how Escher’s imagery transformed over time. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

As the Great Depression reshaped daily life and global tensions mounted, fairs in Chicago, Paris, and New York became spectacular stages where nations expressed optimism, power, and unease through architecture, technology, and performance. In a 3-part series , art historian Jennie Hirsh examines this trio of landmark fairs, revealing how they transformed crisis into dazzling displays that captured both the aspirations and anxieties of their era. title: Becoming Frank Lloyd Wright
desc: Historian and architecture lecturer Bill Keene presents an illustrated look at the life and career of Frank Lloyd Wright. He explores Wright’s Welsh heritage, difficult family life, and early love of nature, then traces the personal and professional triumphs and setbacks that shaped his work. Keene also examines influences including Emerson, Whitman, Louis Sullivan, European architects, and Japanese art, concluding with Wright’s growing fame and business success.

desc: Stamp your calendar for Story Time! Join us every week for a fresh story, a stroll through the Museum, hands-on postal play, and more. Together, we’ll explore mail and all the ways it connects us to people, places, and big ideas. Stop by anytime—whether you stay for one activity or the whole session, this program will get everyone’s “stamp of approval”. Meet in the Museum Lobby. If there are services or accommodations that can improve your experience (e.g., ASL interpretation, etc.), please contact NPMprograms@si.edu ; 1–2 week’s advance notice is recommended but not required.

title: STEAM Career Workshop for Undergraduate Students
desc: Save the date for an exciting opportunity for undergraduate students! Are you curious about careers in science, museums, or research? Want to find an internship or fellowship in a STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Art, Math) field? Join us for a full day of hands-on learning, networking, and behind-the-scenes access to the Smithsonian! Meet museum professionals and explore natural history careers. Freshmen, sophomores, juniors, seniors, and recent grads from community colleges, colleges and universities are invited to sign up for the event. Agenda 10:00 – 10:45 a.m.: Check-in/Welcome/Co

title: The Artists of Renaissance Venice
desc: At the crossroads of the Adriatic, Renaissance Venice was a city shaped by commerce, diplomacy, and cultural exchange. Influences from Byzantium, the Ottoman Empire, and Northern Europe helped foster a distinctly Venetian artistic style, celebrated for its luminous color, sensual beauty, and decorative splendor. Art historian Aneta Georgievska-Shine revisits the works of some of the greatest artists who made Venice one of the most fascinating cultural centers of the Renaissance. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1 credit)

desc: Docents offer interactive programming throughout the museum, in the form of Highlights tours of the museum, gallery spotlight talks, and hands-on cart programs. Tours of the museum’s highlights generally take place daily at 10:15 AM and 1 PM. Additional tours may be offered on the hour between 11 AM and 3 PM as docents are available. Please check either Welcome Desk for today’s schedule. Gallery spotlight talks take place throughout the day. desc: Join us at the Anacostia Community Museum for a cozy story time that brings children, caregivers, and community together through books, creativity, and play. Stories will connect with ACM’s current exhibition and celebrate themes of community, family, neighborhood, history, and the fall and winter seasons. Families are invited to stay for indoor play, creative exploration, and time to connect with one another. This welcoming, accessible program supports different ways of participating, with sensory toys and tools available for children who benefit from tactile, movement, or sensory experiences

Handwork: Contemporary Craft Open House
desc: Join us at SAAM’s Renwick Gallery for a new installation of the contemporary craft collection. See longtime favorites such as Wendell Castle’ s Ghost Clock , as well as works acquired through Handwork: Celebrating American Craft 2026 , an initiative organized by Craft in America . Chat with curatorial staff as well as the artists whose work is on view in the galleries, including Roberto Benavidez , Elizabeth Brim , Vicki Essig , Pat Gorelangton, Chief Bill Harris , Aya Oki , Ato Ribeiro and Diego Romero . Craft activities and a scavenger hunt will be available to provide fun for participants o

title: Castle Docent Tours
desc: Join us for an outdoor tour of the first two buildings in the Smithsonian Institution, the Smithsonian Castle and the Arts & Industries Building (National Museum of the American Latino)! Meet one of our volunteer docents by the sign outside of the north doors of the Castle, on Jefferson Drive SW. Tours subject to volunteer availability and weather conditions; last-minute cancellations may occur. Inquire at the Castle information desk. No registration is required.

title: Highlights Tour
desc: Look for our friendly volunteer at the Information Desk for a 45 minute tour of the highlights of the museum.

title: Tours | Arts of China
desc: Examine the diverse artistic and cultural traditions of one of the world’s oldest civilizations in this in-person, docent-led tour. Learn about Chinese artworks such as ritual bronze vessels, calligraphy, brush paintings in ink and color, and exquisite ceramics. Please meet at the West Building Information Desk for the tour. Dish with foliate flaring rim; Ming dynasty, Xuande reign, 1426–35; Jingdezhen ware; porcelain with cobalt pigment under colorless glaze; H x Diam: 4.8 × 21.3 cm; National Museum of Asian Art, Smithsonian Institution, Freer Collection, Purchase—Charles Lang Freer Endowment

title: Threads of the Viking World: Women’s Lives in Cloth and Craft
desc: A lost mitten. Names carved into spindle whorls. A carefully mended dress laid to rest in a grave. These small, evocative traces open a window into the everyday lives of Viking Age women—lives often missing from the historical record. Historian and broadcaster Eleanor Barraclough draws on archaeological discoveries to reveal the skills, relationships, and identities of women who helped shape the Viking world.

title: Meditation and Mindfulness
desc: Register to join the sessions . Join a free online guided meditation. In these 30-minute sessions, DC-based meditation teachers lead a variety of mindfulness practices. Friday sessions take inspiration from art in our museum’s collections. All are welcome! No previous experience is required. Image credit: Taki Katei / National Museum of Asian Art, Smithsonian Institution, Freer Collection, Gift of Toshio and Yuka Fujikura in memory of Tome Fujikura, F2014.8.28a-d

title: Permanent Collection Tour
desc: The National Museum of Asian Art has over 46,000 artworks from across Asia. Enjoy some of the finest on a docent-led tour and learn about commonalities and differences in cultures, aesthetics, and ideas.

title: Tour | From the Louvre
desc: In From the Louvre: Masterpieces of Islamic Art , you can admire remarkable artworks created between the seventh and nineteenth centuries from a vast geographic area extending from Spain to India. This tour guides you through the exceptional selection of masterpieces, including a striking Syrian-Egyptian basin inlaid with silver figures, an enigmatic Andalusian bronze lion, and a monumental portrait of a Persian king covered with jewels. Meanwhile, learn about the extraordinary journeys these works took and how they were invested with power and new meaning along the way. Image: Signed by Muham

title: Conservation Cart Talk | Preparing Art for Display
desc: The same techniques museums use to care for artwork can help protect treasured items at home. Join paper conservator Kesha Talbert for a behind-the-scenes look at how conservators prepare works on paper for display. Learn about conservation-friendly approaches for displaying photographs, prints, and documents, and see how professional practices can be adapted for personal keepsakes. Image credit: National Museum of Asian Art, Smithsonian Institution, Photo by Department of Conservation and Scientific Research

title: Forward Religions Conference 2026: Welcome Home
desc: FORWARD RELIGIONS CONFERENCE 2026 “Welcome Home” As we commemorate 250 years of Black religious traditions and the 10th anniversary of the Smithsonian’s Center for the Study of African American Religious Life, we recognize both as sacred homes, spaces where Black memory, faith, and cultural life endure. Welcome home to the spaces where Black lives are celebrated, culture thrives, and past, present, and future unite in remembrance, resilience, and resistance.

title: ONLINE | Native Cinema Showcase 2026
desc: The National Museum of the American Indian’s Native Cinema Showcase is an annual celebration of the best in Native film. The festival celebrates the year's best of Indigenous film, spanning documentaries, features, animations, and short-format films by Indigenous filmmakers from across the Western Hemisphere and Arctic. All films will be available to stream free from November 13 (5 PM ET) to November 27, 2026 (5 PM ET).

title: Cinema + Conversation: Montmartre
desc: Fall in love with an evening of cinema and conversation. This Cinema + Conversation features a French-inspired dinner, a screening of Montmartre, and a conversation with the film’s writer and director, Leon Hendrix III, producer Maurice D. Hendrix, and stars Ito Aghayere and Jesse Williams. The evening begins at 5:30 pm with a French-inspired dinner, inviting guests to experience the flavors and atmosphere of France before journeying to Paris through the film. After dinner, guests will head to the Oprah Winfrey Theater for the 7:00 pm screening of Montmartre. Montmartre tells the story of a wo

title: Orchid Diplomacy: How Singapore's Blooms Connect Cultures
desc: Marking 60 years of diplomatic relations between the United States and Singapore in 2026, this special program highlights Singapore’s practice of orchid diplomacy and the Smithsonian’s leadership in orchid research, conservation, and cultivation. Hear from a panel of experts including Smithsonian Gardens Lead Horticulturist Justin Kondrat , who manages the Smithsonian’s Orchid Collection, and Mark Choo , assistant curator at the National Orchid Garden in the Singapore Botanic Gardens. Find out how the naming of orchid hybrids has been used to strengthen relationships between nations, commemora

title: Brewing a Revolution: After Hours
desc: Taverns and coffeehouses have always been more than places to enjoy a drink. From the Colonial era through today, these places bring people together to exchange ideas, discuss local and global events, and engage in the global marketplace. As we celebrate the commemoration of America’s 250th anniversary, we’ll explore the role of taverns and coffeehouses as democratic spaces of civic life, hubs of economic development, and centers of regional and local identity. Join historians and industry experts for a conversation tracing the evolution of these social institutions and their influence on Amer

title: Destiny
desc: Part melodrama, part musical extravaganza, and part plea for religious tolerance, this film by the celebrated Egyptian director Youssef Chahine is the story of the medieval philosopher Ibn-Rashd (known in the West as Averroes). A tireless warrior for free speech, literacy, and rationalism, he strives to preserve the works of Aristotle and other great thinkers while being harassed by conservative clerics. title: Theatre Outing: "Are You Now or Have You Ever Been?"
83rd National Folk Festival
desc: Founded in 1934, the National Folk Festival is the longest-running multicultural celebration of the traditional arts in the United States. The flagship program of the National Council for the Traditional Arts, this traveling festival celebrates the artistic traditions of all Americans and honors the nation’s finest traditional artists. In residence in Jackson, Mississippi, from 2025 to 2027, “the National” features over 300 artists on six stages, nonstop music and dance, parades, a Mississippi folklife area, a family area, regional and international cuisine, and a crafts marketplace.

title: TiE DC - Annual Awards & Diwali Gala 2026
desc: Celebrating Entrepreneurial Excellence, Community & the Festival of Lights Join us for an extraordinary evening of recognition, celebration, and connection at the TiE DC Annual Awards & Diwali Gala 2026!
